title: Mongolia Has Two Economies: One Scans, One Only Takes Tugrik
summary: Ulaanbaatar runs on QR codes while the countryside runs on tugrik cash. Here is how a digital nomad handles everyday spending across both halves of Mongolia in 2026.
body_markdown:
Mongolia will surprise you twice in the same week.


First surprise: Ulaanbaatar is far more cashless than its reputation suggests. Coffee shops near Sukhbaatar Square, lunch spots serving khuushuur, pharmacies, convenience stores, even small kiosks all have QR codes taped to the counter. Locals pay for almost everything by scanning with their phone.


Second surprise: drive two hours out of the city and that entire system vanishes. A ger camp host, a roadside guanz, a driver topping up fuel in a small soum town, they want tugrik banknotes and nothing else.


So the real question for a nomad in Mongolia is not "cash or card." It is "how do I handle a country that is digital in one place and fully cash in the next." Here is the practical split.


## What Payment Looks Like Inside Ulaanbaatar


Walk into almost any shop or restaurant in UB and you will see a QR code, usually a QPay code, sometimes alongside SocialPay or a bank's own app branding. The cashier expects you to scan it, type the amount if it is not preset, and show the confirmation screen.


Card terminals exist too, mostly in bigger supermarkets, hotels, and places like the State Department Store. But plenty of smaller cafes and market stalls skip the card machine entirely. The QR sticker is cheaper for them, so that is what they use.


The catch for visitors: the local apps behind those QR codes are built for residents. They generally want a Mongolian bank account and a local phone number to register. As a foreigner on a tourist stay or even a longer nomad stint, you will usually hit a wall during signup. Mongolia has had few internationally friendly payment options for a long time, and this is exactly why.


## How to Scan Those Same Codes as a Visitor


This is where Moreta Pay closes the gap. It lets you pay through the merchant's standard local QR code, the same one the person ahead of you in line just scanned, without needing a Mongolian bank account or SIM.


The setup is worth doing before you fly in:


- Download the app and verify your identity while you still have fast, familiar internet.


- Connect your home funding source. US banks link via Plaid or ACH, Europeans use SEPA, UK users have Faster Payments, Canadians use e-Transfer, and an international credit or debit card works too.


- Top up your wallet in your own currency.


Then in Ulaanbaatar, paying works like this: open the app, scan the QR on the counter, check the amount, the merchant name, and the FX rate on screen, and confirm. Your balance converts to tugrik and the merchant is paid instantly. No guessing what the conversion cost you, no foreign transaction fee buried on next month's statement. You see the rate before you tap confirm, every time.


That transparency matters more in Mongolia than in most places, because your fallback options are worse here than in, say, Bangkok.


## The Countryside Is a Cash Country, Full Stop


Do not let a smooth week in UB lull you. The moment your trip involves Terelj, the Gobi, Khovsgol, or any multi-day driving tour, you are back to physical tugrik.


Ger camps often take payment on arrival in cash. Roadside canteens, small-town shops, horse guides, hot shower fees at camps, park entry paid at a gate in the middle of nowhere, all cash. Mobile signal is patchy across the steppe, so even a merchant who wanted to offer digital payment often cannot rely on it.


Practical rules that save you grief:


- Withdraw everything you need for the countryside leg before leaving Ulaanbaatar. ATMs outside the capital are scarce and sometimes empty.


- Carry small notes. Breaking a large tugrik bill at a tiny guanz is awkward for everyone.


- Ask your tour operator or driver what is prepaid and what is paid along the way. The answer varies a lot between companies.


- Keep the cash split between your bag and your person. Standard travel sense, but it matters more when the nearest ATM is a day's drive away.

walks through a sensible way to size it without hauling around a nervous-making wad.


## ATMs in Ulaanbaatar: Use Them Strategically, Not Daily


UB has plenty of bank ATMs, and most dispense to foreign cards. But every withdrawal can trigger charges from two directions, your home bank and the machine's operator, which is why pulling out small amounts repeatedly is the most expensive way to fund a trip. We broke down


[why ATM networks charge you twice](https://moretapay.com/blog/why-atm-networks-charge-you-twice-unpacking-the-issuing-bank-fee)


if you want the full picture.


The efficient pattern in Mongolia: use QR payments for everything inside Ulaanbaatar, and make one or two deliberate ATM withdrawals sized for your countryside days. Cash becomes a tool for a specific leg of the trip instead of your default for everything.


## Booking Before You Land, and Paying Bills Once You Stay


For the big-ticket items, book ahead. Flights into Chinggis Khaan International, UB apartments, and tours are easiest sorted online. Moreta Pay also handles QR-based online checkout on platforms like Trip.com and Agoda, so you can settle accommodation from the same wallet you will use at the coffee counter later.


If you settle into Ulaanbaatar for a season, as plenty of nomads do during the pleasant months, the app covers bill payments in supported countries too, which keeps recurring costs out of the cash pile entirely.


## A Working Money Split for a Month in Mongolia


Here is how a typical month shakes out for a nomad splitting time between the capital and a countryside trip:


- **Ulaanbaatar daily life:**


QR payments via your wallet. Coffee, meals, groceries, coworking day passes, taxis arranged through apps. Cash stays in your pocket.


- **Markets and odd edges:**


a little tugrik on hand for the rare stall at Naran Tuul or a street vendor without a code.


- **The countryside leg:**


fully cash, withdrawn in one planned trip to an ATM in UB, carried in small denominations.


- **Bookings and big purchases:**


paid online before travel, through QR checkout where platforms support it.


Two economies, one plan. You scan where Mongolia scans, you pay cash where Mongolia pays cash, and you never find yourself at a ger camp at dusk trying to explain that your money is on your phone.
